Field studies on the Red-billed curassow (Crax blumenbachii) in the lowland Atlantic Forest of Brazil have yielded detailed life-history data for this threatened cracid. Female number two, monitored intensively during the 1981 breeding season, produced a total of 11 eggs over the course of that year, reflecting a maximum reproductive output that was notably high for a species of this body size [Ri = breeding season, produced a total of 11 eggs over the course of that year, reflecting a maximum reproductive output that was notably high for a species of this body size]. Hatchlings emerge with a modest wet weight at birth of approximately 100 grams [Wwb = approximately 100 grams], which represents only a small fraction of the ultimate wet weight attained by adults, a figure that reaches around 3500 grams [Wwi = around 3500 grams] in fully grown individuals. This substantial increase in mass, a more than thirty-fold gain, underscores the rapid growth trajectory characteristic of many galliform birds. The incubation period, documented in captive settings under carefully controlled thermal conditions, required 32 days [ab = 32 days] at a constant 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a temperature that closely mirrors the natural brood patch temperature of the incubating female. Such precise thermal regulation is critical for successful embryonic development in this species.

Longevity records for Crax blumenbachii remain somewhat scarce, but the maximum lifespan in the wild has been estimated from field observations and available capture-mark-recapture data, with the oldest documented individual reaching an age of 11 years [am = 11 years]. This value aligns with the general demographic pattern observed among large cracids, where extended lifespans are often coupled with delayed reproductive schedules. Females do not typically initiate their first breeding attempt until they are relatively old; the time since birth at first brood has been recorded at approximately 1068 days [tR = approximately 1068 days], a substantial delay that likely reflects the prolonged period needed to develop the physical condition and secure the high-quality territories required for successful nesting. This extended pre-reproductive period is a common life-history strategy in species that invest heavily in a small number of offspring per breeding event. The development of the young is similarly staggered, with key ontogenetic milestones occurring over a compressed but critical window following hatching.

The anatomical and physiological transition to adulthood is marked by the onset of adult plumage, a process that initiates relatively late in the species' development. The time since birth at puberty, when the first definitive adult feathers begin to replace the juvenile down, has been estimated at roughly 153 days after hatching [tp = roughly 153 days after hatching]. This molt is not an instantaneous event but a gradual replacement that progresses over several weeks, eventually culminating in the full, sexually dimorphic plumage that characterizes reproductively mature birds. Prior to this point, juveniles exhibit a more cryptic coloration that provides protection against predators during their initial growth phase. Interestingly, despite this extended period before reaching morphological maturity, the chicks themselves are capable of flight remarkably soon after leaving the nest. Field observations confirm that chicks are able to fly at 5 days [tx = 5 days], a surprisingly early age that represents a critical anti-predator adaptation in a forest environment where ground-level threats from mammals and snakes are considerable.

Reproductive investment in Crax blumenbachii is modulated by a combination of environmental and individual factors, and the annual output can be broken down into its constituent components. The maximum reproductive rate observed in the wild, based on the performance of a particularly productive female, equates to an annual effort of approximately 11 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 11 eggs per year]. This is achieved by combining a modest clutch size with a limited number of nesting attempts; specifically, females typically lay two eggs per clutch and can produce a single replacement or second clutch depending on nest success, resulting in up to 5.5 clutches annually under optimal conditions. This strategy of laying few but relatively large eggs is consistent across the Cracidae and is thought to be linked to the high energetic cost of producing a single, heavily-yolked egg that sustains the precocial chick during its early, vulnerable days. The total investment in a single reproductive season, therefore, represents a significant proportion of a female's annual energy budget, a factor that may limit the population's capacity to recover from disturbance.

Comparative analyses across the Cracidae reveal that the life-history parameters of Crax blumenbachii are broadly typical for a forest-dwelling species of its size, although some values are at the slower end of the pace-of-life continuum. The ultimate wet weight of around 3500 grams [Wwi = around 3500 grams] places it among the smaller members of the genus Crax, yet the species demonstrates a remarkably long maximum lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] when compared to other neotropical birds of equivalent mass. This pattern, where a slower life history is allied with a higher risk of extinction, is a hallmark of many threatened avian taxa. The onset of adult plumage at roughly 153 days [tp = roughly 153 days] also situates the species within a moderate developmental window relative to its congeners. Conservation efforts must therefore account for these extended generation times; the delayed age at first brood of nearly three years (approximately 1068 days since birth) [tR = approximately 1068 days since birth] means that populations are slow to replace losses, rendering the species particularly vulnerable to increased adult mortality from hunting or habitat fragmentation. Protecting breeding adults is paramount for the persistence of this iconic bird.
